reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because the creator warns viewers against BitConnectX and criticizes the proposal as a continuation of BitConnect's alleged losses, rather than soliciting investment. The requested viewer action is to avoid participating, as shown by statements such as "Do you want to scam? Because that's how you get a scam" and "Please walk, Go." The website and event footage are presented in the context of explaining and criticizing the third-party scheme.

opening.argument: The material links participation with a financial pathway, rather than merely discussing cryptocurrency. It describes people buying BitConnect tokens so they could place them into BitConnect X, while also saying they had to give the company more money. The associated webpage presents an ICO with login and signup controls, then directs viewers to download a wallet for “storing your wealth.” Together, these elements connect acquiring or converting tokens and taking a concrete wallet action with access to a new token product and its prospective trading market.

citations.quote: the reason people were buying BitConnectToken was because they were going to allow you to take your BitConnect tokens and put those into a new product called Bitconnect X.
So you got to put your hand back in and and give them more of your money.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the video a warning does not erase the participation pathway it presents. The speaker supplies the practical sequence: buy or retain BCC, put it into BitConnect X, and provide more money. The webpage then shows ICO signup and a wallet download explicitly tied to storing wealth. Those details are more than abstract commentary; they make the product and its participation route concrete.

citations.quote: the reason people were buying BitConnectToken was because they were going to allow you to take your BitConnect tokens and put those into a new product called Bitconnect X.
So you got to put your hand back in and and give them more of your money.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quoted sequence is reported as something viewers believed, not an instruction from this speaker. The surrounding language rejects it: “Do you want to scam?” and “Please walk, Go.” A signup screen and wallet download shown in a critical video do not establish that viewers are being solicited by the creator to buy tokens or participate.

opening.argument: The material combines several concrete return signals: BitConnect X is presented as using proof of work and proof of stake, with miners and stakeholders able to earn interest in transaction fees. It also reports a plan in which a roughly $15 entry could lead to coins assigned a value “astronomically higher” than BCC's current street value, with money allegedly available immediately. A financial return tied to staking or holding, paired with an unusually high valuation claim and a low entry figure, is a strong investment solicitation pattern.

citations.quote: you guys were saying that somehow you're gonna buy into this at this nominal rate 15 bucks you're gonna get into this bit Connect X
these coins then had a set value of astronomically higher than the street value
you guys were just going to be pumping money out day one

rebuttal.rebuttal: The fact that the speaker mocks the proposal does not make its return signals disappear. The webpage itself describes interest for miners and stakeholders, while the reported plan combines a nominal entry price, a much higher assigned coin value, and day-one cash extraction. That combination is precisely the risk pattern a careful viewer should treat as promotional financial content, whatever the speaker's tone.

citations.quote: you guys were saying that somehow you're gonna buy into this at this nominal rate 15 bucks you're gonna get into this bit Connect X
these coins then had a set value of astronomically higher than the street value
you guys were just going to be pumping money out day one

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The webpage frame does not supply readable proof of a fixed, passive, or compounding return, and the speaker attributes the $15 and valuation claims to what “you guys were saying.” He then predicts the market will be dumped and calls the proposal a scam. Reporting and criticizing an alleged return is not the same as promising it to viewers.

opening.argument: Although the speaker uses skeptical language, the video repeatedly displays the BitConnect X product, its ICO page, token specifications, exchange interface, wallet download, and a live BitConnect-branded event. This gives viewers a detailed tour of the product's identity, access points, wallet, and proposed exchange availability. The discussion also repeats the proposed token-conversion and value mechanism. In effect, the warning format supplies promotional exposure and a participation map for a token launch.

rebuttal.rebuttal: A critical presentation can still function as promotion when it prominently shows the ICO, exchange, wallet, and branded event while explaining how the token system is supposed to work. The repeated product exposure and concrete access points give viewers information needed to participate, regardless of whether the speaker adds skeptical commentary. The framing therefore does not reliably limit the video's practical effect to education.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The displayed pages are evidence of the third-party proposal's existence, not evidence that the creator endorses it. The spoken content explicitly challenges the proposal, says people are putting in more money, predicts a severe dump, and tells viewers to be wary. Product screenshots in an investigation do not establish a request that this audience participate.
